title.en: The Prophecy of Dipankara and the Young Brahmin Sumedha
title.zh: 燃燈佛授記：婆羅門青年善慧

region.en: The city of Amaravati and the hermitage near Dhammaka in the Himalaya (mythic geography; symbolic pin in the Ganges valley)
region.zh: 阿摩羅城與雪山曇摩伽山仙窟（神話地理；恆河流域象徵性定位）

texts.period: Pali commentarial intro (Nidanakatha) c. 5th c. CE, drawing on the Buddhavamsa; Rhys Davids translation 1880

source.work: Buddhist Birth Stories; or, Dhammapada Commentary intro (Nidanakatha), trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, 1880

summary.en: Four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand cycles before Gotama's birth, the young brahmin Sumedha gives away his inherited fortune, becomes a forest hermit, and gains the meditative powers; meeting the Buddha Dipankara on a muddy road he throws himself down as a living bridge, resolves to become a Buddha himself rather than enter Nirvana as an arhat, and receives Dipankara's public prophecy that he will one day be the Buddha Gotama, son of Maya and Suddhodana — after which he sits all night cataloguing the ten perfections.
summary.zh: 四阿僧祇又十萬劫前，婆羅門青年善慧散盡家財，入雪山為仙人，證得禪定神通；見燃燈佛將臨其城，遂臥泥濘以身作橋供佛經行，並捨阿羅漢之速解，發願成佛；燃燈佛駐足觀其未來，當眾授記：此人必成佛，名喬達摩，母摩耶、父淨飯王云云；善慧遂夜坐逐一省察十波羅蜜。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Jataka/commentarial biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved. Comparative parallel: the cosmic vow-and-prophecy frame parallels quest-immortality heroes across the corpus.

passages.text: Long ages ago there lived in the city of Amaravati a young brahmin named Sumedha, of pure lineage and great learning, whose parents died while he was still young. When the royal steward opened the storehouse and pointed out the wealth of seven generations, Sumedha reflected that his ancestors had carried nothing of it away with them when they died, and it could not be right for him to make taking his wealth with him the aim of his own life. So he proclaimed his intention to the king, gave largesse to the people, and went out from the city to the Himalaya, where he built a hermitage near the mountain Dhammaka and took up the life of a forest ascetic.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Distant Epoch: the story of Sumedha (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: In a single week of strenuous practice Sumedha attained the eight meditative attainments and the five supernatural faculties. While he lived absorbed in their bliss, the Buddha Dipankara appeared in the world, and the city of Ramma decked and levelled the road for his coming. Sumedha, flying down from his hermitage, asked why the people rejoiced, and hearing the word Buddha, begged for a share in the work. They gave him a swampy stretch of the road; he refused to fill it by magic power, choosing instead to labour at it with his own hands. But before he had finished, Dipankara arrived, and Sumedha loosed his matted hair, spread his bark garment and skin mantle in the mire, and lay down like a bridge of jewelled planks, telling the Buddha and his four hundred thousand saints to walk over his body rather than muddy their feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Distant Epoch: the story of Sumedha (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: Lying flat, Sumedha weighed his chances: as a hermit he could destroy the passions that very day and slip quietly into Nirvana as an arhat — or he could resolve, like Dipankara, to reach the supreme truth and then ferry others across the ocean of existence before entering Nirvana himself. He chose the long way, and resolved to become a Buddha. Dipankara, gazing forward through the ages, saw it: in four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand cycles this hermit would be the Buddha Gotama, born in Kapilavatthu, son of Queen Maya and King Suddhodana, served by Ananda, with Upatissa and Kolita as chief disciples, attaining omniscience at the foot of the fig-tree. The assembly rejoiced and made their own prayers for future sanctification; gods and men saluted the 'embryo Buddha'; and Sumedha, seated on a heap of flowers, spent the night investigating the ten perfections, comparing the Buddhas' word to a thrown dice-stick that must fall, to death, to sunrise, to a lion's roar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Distant Epoch: the prophecy of Dipankara (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

texts.language: Pali (commentarial prose interwoven with verse from the Buddhavamsa)
texts.canonical_translation: T. W. Rhys Davids, Buddhist Birth Stories; or, Dhammapada Commentary, vol. 1 (London, Trubner, 1880), the Nidanakatha translation, Distant Epoch (the story of Sumedha, pp. 3-68); the underlying verse is the Buddhavamsa, ed. H. Morris (PTS, 1882)

narrative.en:
The Nidanakatha — the introductory biography that stands before the 547 birth-stories of the Jataka collection — opens its whole narrative with the 'Distant Epoch': the moment the future Gotama first set out on the Buddha-career. That moment is the prophecy of Dipankara, told through the young brahmin Sumedha.

THE RENUNCIATION. Four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand cycles ago (a deliberate, uncountable vastness) there stood the city of Amaravati, ringing with its ten kinds of city-cries. Its brahmin Sumedha was of spotless descent for seven generations, versed in the three Vedas, divination and the traditions. His parents died young; a steward displayed the inherited hoard and told him to guard it. Sumedha reasoned that his ancestors, for all their amassing, had not carried a farthing out of the world; the right course was to make no object of taking one's wealth along. He informed the king, made proclamation, gave largesse, and embraced the hermit's life.

THE REASONING. Seated in the upper chamber he meditated on the grief of rebirth and the breaking-up of the body: 'I am subject to birth, to decay, to disease, to death — it is right, being such, that I should seek the deathless Nirvana, tranquil and free from all these.' He argued that as heat implies cold, existence implies the cessation of existence, and as there is a way out for the man beset by robbers, so there must be a road to Nirvana for the man beset by sin — the fault, if it is not sought, lying with the seeker, not with the road. In a sequence of similes (the filth-heap beside the lotus-lake, the dung carried on the shoulder, the leaky ship, the jewel-plunderer's companion) he counted the advantages of casting off the body, gave away the hoard, and built his hut in the Himalaya, where within seven days of strenuous practice he won the eight attainments and the five supernatural faculties.

THE MEETING. At his conception, birth, enlightenment and first preaching of the Buddha Dipankara, the ten thousand world-systems quaked and the thirty-two prognostics showed themselves; Sumedha, rapt in the bliss of trance, noticed none of it. Dipankara, wandering with a hundred thousand saints, reached the city of Ramma; the citizens decked the streets and levelled the road for him. Flying down from his hermitage, Sumedha asked the reason, heard the word Buddha, and — reckoning how rare the very sound of that word is in the world — asked for a piece of the road to clear himself. Given a swampy stretch, he refused the shortcut of supernatural power: this day it behoved him to perform menial duties, and he fetched earth with his own hands.

THE BRIDGE. Before he had finished, Dipankara came down the decked road, haloed, ray-suffused, attended by four hundred thousand miracle-working saints. Sumedha, seeing that perfection of beauty, thought: this day I will make sacrifice of my life for the Buddha — let him not walk in the mire; let him and his saints trample my body as on a bridge of jewelled planks. He loosed his hair, spread his skin mantle, matted tresses and bark garment in the ink-black mire, and lay down.

THE CHOICE. Lying there he weighed the great alternative that the tradition prizes as the Great Act of Self-Sacrifice: he had it in his power to destroy the passions that very day and enter the city of Ramma a secretly-perfected arhat — Nirvana within grasp. But why, he reasoned, slip unobserved into Nirvana after the destruction of one's own passions only? Better, like Dipankara, to rise to the supreme knowledge of the truth, embark mankind on the ship of the truth and ferry them across the ocean of existence, and only afterwards attain Nirvana. He enumerated the conditions of Buddhahood, made the resolution, and lay still.

THE PROPHECY. Dipankara stood at the hermit's head, opened his eyes like jewelled windows, and cast his prescient gaze forward: in four asankheyyas and a hundred thousand cycles this man will be the Buddha Gotama — his residence Kapilavatthu, his mother Queen Maya, his father King Suddhodana, his chief disciples Upatissa and Kolita, his servitor Ananda, his chief female disciples Khema and Uppalavanna; he will receive a meal of rice-milk at the banyan tree, ascend the throne of Knowledge by the Neranjara, and attain supreme Buddhahood at the Indian fig-tree. The multitudes, hearing the prophecy, were filled with joy — 'an embryo Buddha, the tender shoot that will grow up into a Buddha' — and each recorded a prayer to stand before him in a future life, as men fording a river who miss the opposite ford cross lower down. Dipankara honoured the bodhisattva with eight handfuls of flowers and, reverentially saluting him, departed with all his saints.

THE PERFECTIONS. When all had gone, Sumedha rose from the mire and seated himself cross-legged on a heap of flowers, resolving to investigate the conditions that make a Buddha. The gods of the ten thousand worlds shouted applause: all the omens that attended former bodhisattvas at this moment appeared about him — winds still, rivers stayed, flowers blooming out of season, gems glittering, hell-fires quenched, disease and hunger gone — 'verily thou shalt be Buddha.' Sumedha compared the Buddhas' word to things that cannot fail — a dice-stick thrown into the air must fall, the mortal must die, the sun must rise at dawn — and, searching the ten directions for the path the former bodhisattvas had followed, beheld the first perfection of almsgiving, and began the night-long review of the ten perfections that would carry him, aeon by aeon, to the tree of Bodhi. With this, the Distant Epoch's story is launched: everything in the Jataka book that follows is the working-out of that single act of lying down in the mire.
narrative.zh: 《因緣譚》以「遠因緣」開篇：未來佛陀的漫長求道，始於燃燈佛對善慧仙人的授記。四阿僧祇又十萬劫前，阿摩羅城婆羅門善慧少年失怙，省察先人積財而不能攜走分文，遂散盡家財，入雪山曇摩伽山結庵修行，七日之內證得八定五通。其時燃燈佛出興於世，抵拉摩城，國人修路奉迎；善慧自空而降，聞『佛』之名，求分一段泥濘自任修築，卻不肯以神通完成，寧以凡手運土。佛率四十萬聖眾將至，善慧解髮鋪衣，臥於泥中，願佛與眾踏其身而過，如踏珠板之橋。臥時自忖：今日即可斷盡煩惱，潛入涅槃；然何如如燃燈佛然，先運度眾生，後取菩提？遂發成佛大願。佛立其首邊，以宿命通遠瞻未來，當眾授記：此人四阿僧祇後成佛，名喬達摩，處迦毘羅衛，母摩耶，父淨飯王，侍者阿難云云。天人歡呼『此是佛胎』，各發未來之願。善慧起坐花聚之上，夜省十波羅蜜，以佛語比之擲骰必落、日必東升，深信不疑。此臥泥一舉，遂為全部本生譚之樞紐。

functions: Charter myth of the bodhisattva career: the narrative warrant for the ten perfections (paramitas) and for eons of rebirth in the Jataka collection
Model of heroic self-sacrifice and deferred salvation — the renunciation of immediate Nirvana for the salvation of others
Aetiology of the Buddha-biography program: names in advance every fixed point of the later life (mother, father, city, disciples, tree)
Liturgical anchor: the Sumedha-katha is recited in Theravada countries before ordination and precept ceremonies, binding devotee to the Buddha's long road

variants.name: Buddhavamsa version (the verse source)
variants.text_tradition: Buddhavamsa (Khuddaka Nikaya), with the Nidanakatha as prose commentary
variants.summary: The Buddhavamsa gives the same story in compressed Pali verse, with Sumedha's nine similes and the ten perfections enumerated; the Nidanakatha expands the reasoning and adds the prognostics and the assembly's prayer. Identical prophecy, different rhetorical register.

variants.name: Mahavastu 'Megha' version (Lokottaravadin Sanskrit tradition)
variants.summary: In the Mahavastu the young brahmin is called Megha (or Sumati); he spreads his hair for Dipankara and receives the prophecy, but the pantheon and framing are Mahayanist-leaning and the detail differs — evidence that the prophecy scene was already a shared pan-Buddhist topos reworked by each school.

variants.name: Chinese Lalitavistara-tradition version (Beal)
variants.text_tradition: The Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, trans. Samuel Beal, 1875 (from the Chinese translation of the Lalitavistara tradition)
variants.summary: Beal's version retells the Dipankara episode in the first person within the Buddha's memoirs: the bodhisattva strews the mud with his hair, the earth quakes six times, and Dipankara predicts his Buddhahood — the same bridge-scene, but placed inside a northern biographical frame rather than as the opening of a commentary.

primary_sources.citation: Buddhist Birth Stories; or, Dhammapada Commentary, vol. 1, trans. T. W. Rhys Davids (London 1880), translation pp. 1-90 (the story of Sumedha, pp. 3-68); PTS edition of the Jatakatthavannana: ed. V. Fausboll, Jataka vol. 1 (1877), Nidanakatha pp. 1-90.
Khuddaka Nikaya; ed. H. Morris, PTS 1882 — the verse source of the Sumedha story that the Nidanakatha glosses.

secondary_sources.work: Andre Foucher, The Life of the Buddha, According to the Iconography of the Early Buddhist Sculptures of India
secondary_sources.citation: Foucher 1963 (English translation of the 1908 French; Munshiram Manoharlal/New Delhi and Calcutta) — classic study of how the Nidanakatha episodes map onto early Gandhara and Bharhut sculpture, incl. the Dipankara and Sumedha scenes.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The text belongs to the Pali commentarial canon of a still-living Theravada tradition and is freely taught, recited and retold; present it as a scholarly record of the tradition's own narrative, not as adjudication of its truth-claims. Note for curators: the Sumedha-prophecy is recited liturgically in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia at ordination and precept ceremonies; avoid comic or dismissive framing of the mud-bridge scene, which is treated as the paradigmatic act of devotion.

title.en: The Descent from Tushita and Maya's Dream of the White Elephant
title.zh: 兜率下生與摩耶夫人夢白象入胎

region.en: Kapilavastu, capital of the Sakyas (pin at the Lumbini complex nearby)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛城，釋迦族之都（附近藍毘尼聖區定位）

texts.period: Pali commentarial intro (Nidanakatha) c. 5th c. CE; Rhys Davids translation 1880

source.work: Buddhist Birth Stories; or, Dhammapada Commentary intro (Nidanakatha), trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, 1880

summary.en: The future Buddha, waiting in the heaven of Delight, surveys the five things that determine a Buddha's birth — continent, district, town, caste and mother — chooses Jambudvipa, Kapilavastu, the warrior caste and Queen Maya, and descends to be conceived. At the midsummer festival Maya dreams that four guardian spirits carry her to the Himalaya, bathe her at the Anotatta lake, and lodge her in a golden mansion, where a superb white elephant with a white lotus in its trunk circles her couch three times and enters her right side; sixty-four brahmins read the dream, and thirty-two portents light up the ten thousand worlds.
summary.zh: 未來佛居兜率天，省察決定佛誕之五事——洲、域、城、種姓、母——擇閻浮提、迦毘羅衛、剎帝利種與摩耶夫人，允諾天眾後下生入胎。仲夏節慶之夜，四大天王舉床攜夫人至雪山，阿耨達池沐浴更衣，安置金宮；白象口銜白蓮，三匝其床，自右脅入；翌日六十四位婆羅門解夢，十萬世界現三十二瑞相。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Waiting in the heaven of Delight (Tushita), the future Buddha saw that the time of his advent had arrived. Reflecting on where Buddhas appear, he fixed on Jambudvipa; on the district, the Middle Country; on the town, Kapilavastu; on the caste, the Kshatriyas, then predominant — and on Suddhodana as father. Reflecting on the mother, he chose Mahamaya, who had kept the five precepts from birth and had fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand ages, foreseeing that her life would last ten months and seven days more. Having thus decided the five great points, he granted the deities their prayer — 'the time has arrived for me to become a Buddha' — and attended by the angels of the heaven of Joy, descended and was conceived in the womb of the Lady Mahamaya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the descent and conception (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the midsummer festival Queen Maya, radiant and uninebriated, rose early on the seventh day, bathed in perfumed water, distributed four hundred thousand pieces in alms, and vowed the eight commandments. Lying on her royal couch she dreamt: the four guardian angels of the world lifted her bed and carried her to the Himalaya, set her beneath the great sala-tree, and their queens bathed her in the lake Anotatta and decked her in heavenly garments. Near the Silver Hill they lodged her in a golden mansion; and the future Buddha, become a superb white elephant wandering the Golden Hill, descended, approached from the north, and holding in his silvery trunk a white lotus flower, thrice circled his mother's couch doing obeisance, gently struck her right side, and seemed to enter her womb. He was conceived at the end of the midsummer festival.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: Maha Maya's dream (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning she told the dream to the king, who summoned sixty-four eminent brahmins, feasted them on milk-rice and gifts, and asked what would come of it. They answered: be not anxious; the queen has conceived a man-child who, if he keeps the householder's life, will become a universal monarch, but if he leaves home will become a Buddha and remove the veils of ignorance and sin from the world. At the moment of incarnation the ten thousand world-systems quaked; an immeasurable light appeared; the blind saw, the deaf heard, the lame walked, prisoners were freed, hell-fires went out, and every instrument sounded unplayed. Four angels with swords guarded mother and child; and because a womb once occupied by a future Buddha is like a relic-shrine never to be reused, Maya died seven days after the birth and was reborn in the heaven of Delight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the dream interpreted, the omens (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

title.en: The Birth in the Lumbini Grove and the Seven Steps
title.zh: 藍毘尼園降誕與七步宣言

region.en: Lumbini grove, between Kapilavastu and Devadaha (modern Lumbini, Nepal)
region.zh: 藍毘尼園，迦毘羅衛與天臂城之間（今尼泊爾藍毘尼）

texts.period: Pali commentarial intro (Nidanakatha) c. 5th c. CE; Rhys Davids translation 1880

source.work: Buddhist Birth Stories; or, Dhammapada Commentary intro (Nidanakatha), trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, 1880

summary.en: Ten months pregnant, Queen Maya sets out for her family home and stops in the Lumbini grove, where the sala-tree bends its branch down to her hand and she is delivered standing. Great Brahma receives the babe on a golden net; the newborn stands erect and unsullied, takes seven strides and proclaims himself chief of the world under Sakka's umbrella; the Connatal Ones come into being with him, and the seer Kaladevala, summoned from heaven, does homage to the infant and then weeps that he will not live to see him enlightened.
summary.zh: 夫人懷胎十月，赴母家途中入藍毘尼園，手扶娑羅樹枝，站立誕子。大梵天以金網承之；嬰兒無染而立，東南西北各行一步，於第七步止，帝釋張傘，天眾持王室象徵隨侍，兒發獅吼：『吾為世間之最。』與之俱生者七事（駟馬、象、侍者、藏瓶等）同時出現；仙人迦羅延瓦從天而下，拜此嬰兒，又泣言不能親見其成佛。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Other women give birth sitting or lying, some before and some after ten months; the mother of a future Buddha delivers standing, after exactly ten months. Queen Maya, her time fulfilled, wished to go to her family home at Devadaha; the king consented, made the road plain, and sent her in a golden palanquin with a thousand attendants. Between the two towns lay the Lumbini grove of sala-trees, at that season one mass of fruit and flowers from root to topmost branch, humming with bees and birds. Entering the wood, she reached for the branch of the monarch sala-tree; it bent down to her hand like a reed heated by steam, her pains came upon her, and standing and holding the branch she was delivered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the birth in Lumbini (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: At that instant four pure-minded Great Brahma angels came bringing a golden net, received the child on it, and set him before his mother: 'Be joyful, O Lady! a mighty son is born to thee!' He left the womb as a preacher steps from a pulpit — erect, unsoiled, shining like a gem on Benares muslin — while two showers of water fell from heaven to refresh him. Four kings received him on antelope skins, then men on fine cloth; and set on the ground he looked toward the East, where thousands of world-systems lay open to his sight like a single courtyard. Finding none like himself in the ten directions, he took seven strides, saying 'This is the best direction,' with Great Brahma holding the white umbrella over him and Sakka following with the fan; and at the seventh step he stopped and sent forth his noble voice in the shout of victory: 'I am the chief of the world.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the seven steps (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: At his birth seven things came into being with him — the mother of Rahula, the attendant Channa, the minister Kaludayi, the royal horse Kanthaka, the great Bo-tree and four vase-treasures — the Connatal Ones. The gods of the Tavatimsa heaven rejoiced, telling one another that a son was born to Suddhodana who seated under the Bo-tree would become a Buddha. The ascetic Kaladevala, resting in heaven, heard their joy, descended, and asked to see the child; but when they bore the babe forward to salute him, the infant turned his feet so that they rested on the ascetic's matted hair — no one alive was worthy of the bodhisattva's salutation, and the ascetic's head would have split otherwise. Rising from his seat, Kaladevala did homage to the child, and the king, seeing the wonder, did homage to his own son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the Connatal Ones and Kaladevala's homage (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

title.en: The Four Signs: Old Man, Sick Man, Corpse and Renunciate
title.zh: 四相：老者、病者、死者與出家人

region.en: The roads between Kapilavastu and its pleasure-gardens (pin at the Lumbini/Kapilavastu complex)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛至林苑間的官道（藍毘尼／迦毘羅衛聖區定位）

texts.period: Pali commentarial intro (Nidanakatha) c. 5th c. CE; Rhys Davids translation 1880

source.work: Buddhist Birth Stories; or, Dhammapada Commentary intro (Nidanakatha), trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, 1880

summary.en: The brahmins at the name-giving had foretold that the prince would renounce the world on seeing four signs; Suddhodana thereupon posted guards to keep all four away. But the gods, deciding the time for enlightenment had come, created an aged man, then a sick man, then a corpse on the prince's drives, visible to him alone; each sight turned him home in anguish, while his father doubled the concerts and guards. Only the fourth sign — a mendicant, described by a divinely inspired charioteer — he carried into the pleasure-garden with him. That evening Kisa Gotami's song from the rooftop told him his own future wife was envied, and Rahula was named 'Impediment.'
summary.zh: 命名之日婆羅門預言：王子見四相必出家；淨飯王遂四門設衛，禁四相近身。然諸天以開悟時機已至，先後幻現老人、病人、死人於王子出遊之道上，唯王與御者得見；每一相皆令王子悲返王宮，王乃倍增樂事與守衛。唯第四相——出家人——經御者（蒙天力所感）解說，王子攝心入苑。當晚基沙瞿曇彌於屋頂歌詠，佛陀聞之歌悟無常，遂有離世之志；耶輸陀羅生子，命名『障礙』。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: At the name-giving the eight brahmins read the babe's signs: seven raised two fingers — universal monarch or Buddha — but the young Kondanna raised one finger only: 'There is no sign of his remaining amidst the cares of household life; verily, he will become a Buddha.' Asked after what sights the prince would renounce the world, they answered: after the four omens — a man worn out by age, a sick man, a dead body, and a monk. Suddhodana posted guards along the roads to keep all four from his son's sight, built him three mansions for the three seasons with forty thousand dancing girls, and waited. One day, when the prince set out for the pleasure-ground, the angels thought: the time for his enlightenment is near, let us show him the omens — and made a son of the gods appear as a man wasted by age, visible to the prince and charioteer alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the prophecy of the four omens, the first sign (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'What kind of man is this, whose hair is not as that of other men?' the prince asked. The charioteer answered that this is old age, and that it had come on the man step by step as it would come on them all. 'Shame then on life,' said the prince, 'since the decay of every living being is notorious!' and, agitated, he turned back at that very spot and re-entered his palace. The king, hearing the cause, ordered concerts to be multiplied and the guards pushed further out. Another day the gods showed a sick man, and the prince turned home again with his heart agitated; another day a dead man borne along the road — again he turned back, and again the king increased the music and the guard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the second and third signs (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: A fourth drive brought a man who had abandoned the world, decently clad. There being no Buddha in the world, the charioteer did not know what a mendicant was, but inspired by the gods he answered, 'That is a mendicant friar,' and described the advantages of renouncing the world — and that day the prince, cherishing the thought of renunciation, went on to the pleasure-ground. (Some teachers say he saw all four omens the same day.) At sunset, as attendants decked him on the royal stone, a noble virgin named Kisa Gotami watched from her roof and burst into song: 'Blessed indeed the mother, blessed the father, blessed the wife, who owns so glorious a lord!' Hearing it, the future Buddha asked what could give every heart lasting peace; the answer came that peace is won when the fires of lust, hatred and delusion go out — and he resolved to renounce the world that very day, sending the girl a pearl-string as a teacher's fee. Word came that a son was born to him; 'An impediment has arisen,' he said, 'a bond' — and the king named the child Rahula, Impediment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the fourth sign, Kisa Gotami's song, Rahula's name (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

title.en: The Great Renunciation: the Sleeping Dancers, Kanthaka, and the Night Flight
title.zh: 大出家：睡舞伎、健陟馬與夜遁

region.en: Kapilavastu to the river Anoma, thirty leagues (pin at the Lumbini/Kapilavastu complex)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛至阿諾摩河，三十由旬（藍毘尼／迦毘羅衛聖區定位）

texts.period: Pali commentarial intro (Nidanakatha) c. 5th c. CE; Rhys Davids translation 1880

source.work: Buddhist Birth Stories; or, Dhammapada Commentary intro (Nidanakatha), trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, 1880

summary.en: Waking in the third watch to find his dancers asleep in grotesque attitudes, the prince sees the palace as a charnel-house and resolves on the Great Renunciation that very day. He mounts the white horse Kanthaka while the gods muffle its neigh and catch its footfall in their palms; the gate-spirit opens the barred gate, Mara offers him the wheel of empire in seven days and is refused, and the city revolves on its axis so he can gaze his last farewell. At the Anoma river he cuts off his hair, which Sakka receives into a jeweled casket; the archangel Ghatikara supplies the mendicant's eight requisites; Kanthaka dies of a broken heart, and after meeting Bimbisara in Rajagaha the bodhisattva promises to return and teach after his enlightenment.
summary.zh: 王子半夜醒來，見舞伎橫陳酣睡、種種醜態，視王宮如停屍房，決意當日行大出家。神明掩其馬嘶、以掌承其蹄聲，跨健陟白馬越城；門神啟閉鎖之門，魔王於空中許以七日後轉輪王位，遭拒；大地旋轉使王子回望城邑作別。至阿諾摩河削髮，帝釋以寶函收其髻冠；天人曇給八資具；健陟馬聞訊傷心而死；至王舍城，頻毘娑羅王勸王位不成，求佛成道後先來度化，許之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: That evening, after Kisa Gotami's song, women lovely as heavenly nymphs danced and played before the prince; but his heart, estranged from sin, took no pleasure, and he fell asleep. The women, seeing him asleep, laid aside their instruments and lay down too. Waking in the third watch, he saw them sprawled around the guttering lamps — some foaming at the mouth, some grinding their teeth, some muttering, some with dress in disorder — plainly revealed as horrible sources of mental distress. The splendid chamber seemed a charnel-house full of loathsome corpses, and life itself like a house the prey of devouring flames. 'It all oppresses me! It is intolerable!' — and he resolved that very day to accomplish the Great Renunciation. Passing to Rahula's chamber he found the child asleep on his mother's hand; unwilling to wake her, he thought 'I will come back and see him when I have become a Buddha,' and left the palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the sleeping dancers and the resolve (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: Channa saddled the mighty white horse Kanthaka, who knew what the saddling meant and neighed a neigh the gods smothered so none could hear; at each step they caught the hoof-fall in the palms of their hands. With Channa holding the tail, they reached the great gate at midnight. The king had set a thousand men at each gate; the gate-spirit opened it of his own accord — else one of the three, master, servant or horse, had leapt the eighteen-cubit rampart. Then Mara stood in the air to stop him: 'Depart not! In seven days the wheel of empire will appear and make you sovereign of the four continents!' — 'I know it well; but I do not desire sovereignty. I will become a Buddha and make the ten thousand world-systems shout for joy.' From that hour the Tempter followed him like a shadow, watching for any slip. As the prince turned to gaze a last time, the broad earth revolved like a potter's wheel and stayed, turning the city back into his view.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the night flight and Mara's temptation (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: Angels carried torches before, behind and on either side, and the sky rained Paricchattaka flowers as the bodhisattva crossed three kingdoms that one night to the river Anoma. Kanthaka, despite his power, had been delayed hauling through the cast-down garlands, and managed but thirty leagues. At the river the horse sprang its five-hundred-yard breadth at a press of the heel; the prince dismounted on the silver sand, gave back horse and ornaments to Channa — who three times begged to renounce the world too — and cut off his own plaited hair and diadem with his sword, throwing them skyward. Sakka caught them in a jewelled casket and set them in Tavatimsa; the archangel Ghatikara, his friend of a former Buddha-age, brought the eight requisites of a mendicant. Kanthaka, listening till the last, died of a broken heart and was reborn an angel. Seven days in the Anupiya mango-grove, then on foot thirty leagues to Rajagaha, where King Bimbisara, offering him his kingdom in vain, obtained the promise: after my Buddhahood I will come to your kingdom first.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the Anoma river, the hair-offering, Bimbisara (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

title.en: Sujata's Milk-Rice and the Golden Bowl

region.en: Uruvela on the Neranjara river, near the Bodhi-tree (modern Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 優樓頻螺尼連禪河畔，菩提樹側（今菩提伽耶）

texts.period: Pali commentarial intro (Nidanakatha) c. 5th c. CE; Rhys Davids translation 1880

source.work: Buddhist Birth Stories; or, Dhammapada Commentary intro (Nidanakatha), trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, 1880

summary.en: Six years of the Great Struggle have left the bodhisattva skeletal and have driven away his five companions; perceiving that penance is not the way, he takes ordinary food again. In the village of Senani, the landowner's daughter Sujata — whose prayer for a husband and son made at a nigrodha-tree has been answered — prepares the year's offering by working the milk in and in from a thousand cows down to eight; the gods light her fire and infuse the sap of life into the very pot. Her slave-girl finds the ascetic glowing at the tree's foot, takes him for the tree-god, and Sujata pours the milk-rice into his hands. Divided into forty-nine balls, it is the only food for the forty-nine days to enlightenment; the golden vessel, thrown into the river as an omen, swims upstream and is received by the snake-king Kala among the bowls of the former Buddhas.
summary.zh: 六年苦行使未來佛形銷骨立，五侍者失望而去；悟苦行非道，乃受常食。舍那尼村主之女善生，昔於尼拘陀樹下祈願得遂，備歲供：千牛之乳層層熬煉，天人司火、注入命氣。侍女見樹下放光之聖者，誤為樹神；善生以金缽盛乳糜奉之。分為四十九丸，為成道前四十九日唯一飲食；擲缽入河為徵，金缽逆流而上，為蛇王迦羅所收，與前三佛之缽同列。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The bodhisattva had resolved to perform the uttermost penance, living at last on a single grain or seed a day — while the angels, gathering the sap of life, infused it into him through the pores of his skin. He became thin as a skeleton; his golden colour darkened; the thirty-two marks of a Great Being vanished; and one day, overcome by pain, he fainted to the ground. Some angels reported him dead, and Suddhodana refused to believe it. Recovering, the Great Being perceived that penance was not the way to wisdom, begged ordinary food again, and his golden complexion returned. The five mendicants who had served him six years concluded that spiritual advantage was not to be got from him — like hoping to bathe one's head in a dew-drop — and left him for Isipatana near Benares.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the failure of penance (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Uruvela, in the village of Senani, lived Sujata, daughter of the landowner Senani, grown to marriageable age. She had vowed to a nigrodha-tree: if she were married into a family of equal rank and had a son for her firstborn, she would spend a hundred thousand every year on an offering to the tree; and her prayer took effect. On the full-moon day of May, in the sixth year of the Great Struggle, she made the offering — driving a thousand cows into rich pasture and working the milk in and in, from the thousand to five hundred, two hundred and fifty, and so down to eight. Early that morning she milked the eight; of their own accord the calves kept away, and streams of milk poured of themselves into the new vessels; when the rice-milk boiled, huge bubbles ran to the right, no drop was lost, and no smoke rose from the fire, which the four guardian angels kept watch over and Great Brahma canopied, while Sakka put the sticks together — and the gods, crushing the honey from the comb of the four continents' life-sap, infused it into the vessel itself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: Sujata's offering (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wondering at so many marvels on one day, Sujata sent her slave-girl Punna to watch the holy place; Punna found the bodhisattva at the foot of the tree, lighting up the region with his glory, and ran back with the news that their god had descended to receive the offering in his own hand. Sujata filled a golden vessel worth a hundred thousand, advanced bowing, and placed it in the ascetic's right hand, saying, 'May there arise to thee as much joy as has come to me,' and went her way, valuing the vessel no more than a dried leaf. He bathed in the Neranjara, divided the rice into forty-nine balls, and ate — the only food of the seven weeks to come. Then he threw the golden bowl into the river as an omen: 'If I shall be a Buddha to-day, let it go up the stream.' It swam eighty cubits against the current, dived to the palace of the snake-king Kala, and struck against the bowls of the three former Buddhas — 'Yesterday a Buddha arose, to-day another has arisen' — and sank to rest as the lowest of them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Intermediate Epoch: the offering made, the bowl omen (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

title.en: The First Sermon at Benares: the Turning of the Wheel

region.zh: 波羅奈附近的鹿野苑仙人住處

texts.period: Pali commentarial intro (Nidanakatha) c. 5th c. CE; Rhys Davids translation 1880

source.work: Buddhist Birth Stories; or, Dhammapada Commentary intro (Nidanakatha), trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, 1880

summary.en: After the seven weeks under the Bo-tree — Mara's daughters worsted, the merchants' honey-cakes and the four bowls joined into one — the Buddha hesitates whether a truth so deep can be told; Great Brahma comes with a thousand rulers of the heavens to beg the preaching, and the Buddha, finding his old teachers dead, sets out for the five mendicants at Benares. They resolve not to honour him but are overcome by the radiance of his love; he announces his Buddhahood, preaches the discourse called the Fundaments of the Kingdom of Righteousness, Kondanna gains the First Path, and within days all five are Arahats — after which the sixty are sent out to teach, the Kassapas are won by three thousand five hundred miracles, and Bimbisara gives the Bambu Grove, whose acceptance makes the earth shake: the Religion of Buddha has taken root.
summary.zh: 七周已過，魔王之女敗退；帝釋獻蜜餅，四天王各奉寶石之缽，四缽合而為一。佛思法深難解，躊躇不說；大梵天率諸天懇請轉法輪。舊師阿羅邏、鬱陀迦已卒，乃往波羅奈度五比丘。五人約不致敬，然佛慈光所被，不由自主起迎禮拜。佛自證佛果，說《轉法輪經》（初轉法輪之教），憍陳如於說法中得初果；不數日五人皆成阿羅漢。繼而六十羅漢分遣四方，以三千五百神通降三迦葉，頻毘娑羅王獻竹林精舍；受供之時大地震動——佛陀之教已生根。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Seven weeks the Buddha spent in the joy of salvation: Mara's three daughters — Craving, Discontent and Lust — tried him in a hundred forms and returned defeated, confessing that such things might be done in the presence of men who linger in the paths of sin, but against him they availed nothing. On the last day two merchants, Tapassu and Bhalluka, offered rice-cake and honey-cake; the four guardian angels brought bowls of sapphire and jet, which at the Buddha's word closed into one with only the seam-lines visible. Returning to the Shepherd's Nigrodha-tree, he was filled with the doubt that comes to every Buddha — that he lacked the ability to make a truth so deep and subtle intelligible to others. Then the great Ruler of the Brahma-heavens, crying 'Alas! the world is lost!', brought the rulers and archangels of ten thousand world-systems to beg the preaching of the Truth, and the Master granted the request.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Proximate Epoch: the seven weeks and Brahma's plea (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: Considering to whom he should first reveal the Truth, he thought of Alara his former teacher, but Alara had died seven days before; Uddaka died that very evening. So he fixed on the five mendicants who had served him faithfully, perceiving that they were in the Deer-forest at Benares, and determined 'There I will go to inaugurate the Kingdom of Righteousness.' On the way the ascetic Upaka asked whether he was a god or a spirit or a man; he announced himself a Buddha, conqueror of all. The five, seeing him coming from afar, agreed to offer him no reverence — but as he drew near, the sense of his love diffused itself through their hearts until, unable to hold to their resolve, they rose and welcomed him. He announced to them his Buddhahood — 'address not a Buddha by his name, or as brother: I, mendicants, am a Buddha' — and taught them the discourse called the Fundaments of the Kingdom of Righteousness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Proximate Epoch: the journey and the arrival at Isipatana (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.

passages.text: As the discourse went on, Kondanna the Believer gained the Fruit of the First Path; day by day the other four followed, and on the fifth day the Master preached On the Non-existence of the Soul, at the end of which all five attained Nirvana. Then the young noble Yasa was won with 'Follow me!' and his fifty-four companions with him, till there were sixty-one Arahats in the world; the Buddha sent out the sixty with the words 'Go forth, mendicants, preaching and teaching.' Overcoming at Uruvela the three fire-worshipping Kassapa brothers with three thousand five hundred miracles, attended by their thousand disciples he went to Rajagaha, redeemed his promise to Bimbisara, and accepted the Bambu Grove — at whose acceptance the broad earth shook, as if to say, 'Now the Religion of Buddha has taken root!' There Sariputta and Moggallana, hearing a single verse from the Elder Assaji, were converted and were later made the two chief disciples.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhist Birth Stories (Nidanakatha), Proximate Epoch: the five disciples, the sending of the sixty, the founding of Rajagaha (Rhys Davids 1880); not verbatim.
